title: 38-38_Vermont State Employees' Association v. Vermont Department of Human Resources and Department of Corrections
text:
VERMONT LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
VERMONT STATE EMPLOYEES’
ASSOCIATION DOCKET NO. 22-39
v.
STATE OF VERMONT,
DEPARTMENT OF HUMAN
RESOURCES AND DEPARTMENT
OF CORRECTIONS
FINDINGS OF FACT, OPINION, AND ORDER
The Vermont State Employees’ Association, Inc. (“VSEA”) filed an unfair labor practice
charge alleging that the State violated 3 V.S.A. § 961(1) and (5) when it refused to bargain with
the VSEA and “bypassed the bargaining agent by communicating directly with VSEA unit
members and bargained in the press.” VSEA requests as a remedy that this Board order the State
to cease and desist, and to make whole any affected employees for their losses. The State filed a
response to the charge and a motion to dismiss. On October 8, 2024, the Vermont Labor
Relations Board issued an Unfair Labor Practice Complaint.
The parties provided stipulated facts and presented briefs to the Board Panel comprised
of David Boulanger, Acting Chair, Alan Willard, and Michelle Phelps.
FINDINGS OF FACT
Parties
1. The Vermont State Employees' Association, Inc. ("VSEA") is an employee organization
as that term is defined in 3 V.S.A. §902(6) with offices at 155 State Street, Montpelier,
Vermont 05602, and is the certified collective bargaining agent for the Supervisory and
Corrections Bargaining Units of the Executive Branch of the State of Vermont.
38

2. The State of Vermont is an employer herein as that term is defined in 3 V.S.A. §902(7)
and is represented for collective bargaining by the Department of Human Resources, with
a principal office at 120 State Street in Montpelier, Vermont 05620.
3. The employer herein is the State of Vermont and its Department of Corrections (“DOC”)
and Department of Human Resources (“DHR”) (collectively referred to as “the State”).
Facts relating to the Unfair Labor Practice Charge
4. At all times relevant herein, the VSEA and the State have been parties to collective
bargaining agreements for the Supervisory and Corrections Bargaining Units
(“Contracts”) in effect for the period from July 1, 2020 to June 30, 2022, and July 1, 2022
to June 30, 2024. See Exhibits A1, A2, B1, and B2.
5. The Contracts include articles titled “Management Rights” that include the following
provisions:
The parties will negotiate as required by law over any dispute arising under
paragraph 1, provided said condition of employment is a mandatory bargaining
subject. The parties shall meet within ten (10) days (unless mutually agreed to
extend) after a request for negotiations by either party and thereafter on a regular
basis. At the end of a forty-five (45) calendar day period, which shall commence
with the beginning of negotiations, the State may implement any proposed change
or new condition of employment, whether or not the parties will have bargained to
genuine impasse. The VSEA shall retain all statutory impasse procedure rights as
may be lawfully available to VSEA during the life of this Agreement except as
otherwise provided in the Employee Workweek/Work Location/Work Shift
Article. With respect to any dispute under paragraphs 2, 3, and 4, the parties agree
that they have fully bargained and any disputes thereunder will be processed
according to the grievance procedure.
See Exhibit A1, A2, B1, and B2, all at Article 2.5
6. The Contracts include articles titled “Employee Workweek/Work Location/Work Shift”
that include the following provisions:
2. NEW SHIFTS/WORKWEEK
In any department or institution, prior to establishment of a new shift (a shift with
starting and quitting time different from any existing shift) or a new workweek (a
39

combination of workdays constituting forty (40) hours (or eighty (80)) hours
biweekly if applicable) which is different from any existing combination of
workdays, or which includes evenings or half days, the State shall notify the
VSEA and will meet, if requested within ten (10) days, on a regular basis to
negotiate the impact of this decision for up to forty-five (45) calendar days. At the
end of the forty-five (45) calendar day period commencing from the date VSEA
requests negotiations the State may implement its proposed new shift or new
workweek without further negotiations or recourse to the statutory impasse
procedure.
See Exhibit A1, A2, B1, and B2, Article 20.2.
7. No shift or work week exceeding 40 hours in a week or 80 hours biweekly has been
created or established within the bargaining units without agreement of the Parties or
through the imposition of a contract by the VLRB.
8. DHR Labor Relations Director John Berard’s July 5, 2022 communication to VSEA’s
Executive Director Steve Howard and Director of Labor Relations Gary Hoadley
referenced at Paragraph 9 of the Charge is attached as Exhibit C.
9. Commissioner Deml’s July 6, 2022 communication to all DOC employees referenced at
Paragraph 10 of the Charge is attached as Exhibit D.
10. The State’s July 6, 2022 press release titled “Vermont DOC to Implement ‘Stability and
sustainability’ Plan referenced at Paragraph 11 of the Charge is attached as Exhibit E.
11. VSEA Director of Labor Relations Gary Hoadley’s message to DHR Director of Labor
Relations John Berard referenced in Paragraph 12 of the Charge is attached as Exhibit F.
12. The email communication between Mr. Berard and Mr. Hoadley transmitting Exhibits C
and F, herein, is attached as Exhibit G.
13. On July 28, 2022, the parties executed a side letter specifying certain temporary schedule
changes, recruitment and retention bonus and other monetary enhancements for
employees in the bargaining units. The parties met and discussed the contents of the side
letter in advance of executing the side letter. See Exhibit H.
40

14. On August 2, 2022, Mr. Berard rescinded his July 5, 2022, letter because “DOC no
longer intend[ed] to establish the new work shifts/schedules described therein.” See
Exhibit I.
15. To date, the State has not retracted its July 6, 2022 communication from Commissioner
Deml to all DOC employees. See Paragraph 10 of the Charge.
16. To date, the State maintains its July 6, 2022 press release titled “Vermont DOC to
Implement ‘Stability and Sustainability’ Plan” on its public website. See Paragraph 11 of
the Charge; see also: https://doc.vermont.gov/press-release/vermont-doc-implement-
stability-and-sustainability-plan.
OPINION
The Union asserts the State of Vermont Department of Corrections, (“State” “DOC”)
violated the State Employees Labor Relations Act (“SELRA”), 3 V.S.A § 961 (a)(1) and (5),
when DOC communicated directly with its represented employees on July 6, 2022, to the
exclusion of the Union, and communicated to the press regarding changes to the working
conditions before providing the Union any opportunity to negotiate a mandatory subject of
bargaining. The State responds that it did not decline or refuse to negotiate because it informed
the Union representative of the change in work hours, “absent a request to bargain” the impact of
that change. The State also claims the Commissioner’s email was not an attempt to deal directly
with employees or circumvent the Union, and that it did not denigrate or undercut the authority
of VSEA with its members. Finally, the State asserts that because the parties have successfully
bargained the shift change, the matter is moot and the Board lacks jurisdiction.
The charging party has the burden of proving by a preponderance of the evidence that an
unfair labor practice occurred. See 3 V.S.A § 965(d); Castleton Education Association, Vermont-
41

NEA v. Castleton-Hubbardton Board of School Directors, 13 VLRB 60, 66 (1990). It is an unfair
labor practice for the State to interfere with, restrain, or coerce employees in the exercise of their
bargaining rights. 3 V.S.A. § 961(1). It is an unfair labor practice for the State to refuse to
collectively bargain with designated representatives of employees. 3 V.S.A. § 961 (5). Working
conditions are mandatory subjects of bargaining under 3 V.S.A. § 904 (a)(3). Work schedules
which constitute working conditions are mandatory bargaining subjects of bargaining. VSEA v.
State of Vermont (re: Implementation of a “6-2” Schedule at VT. State Hospital), 5 VLRB 303,
13 (1982). Unilateral changes in mandatory subjects of bargaining “is the very antithesis of
bargaining and is a per se violation of the duty to bargain.” Essex Junction Education
Association v. Essex Junction Prudential Committee, 14 VLRB 107, 119 (1991).
Although the Board has not considered whether and under what circumstances direct
communication between management and members of a collective bargaining unit constitutes an
unfair labor practice, the Board has resolved the issue when applying the Municipal statute. The
Board has held that “school boards do not improperly circumvent the bargaining representative
and do not bargain in bad faith if direct communications with employees are non-coercive and
contain ‘no threat of reprisal or promise of benefit.’” Colchester Education Association v.
Colchester Board of Education, 19 VLRB 108, 11 (1996) (quoting Burlington Education Ass’n
v. Burlington Bd of School Commissioners, 7 VLRB 248, 250-51 (1984)(internal quotations
omitted)). The Board considers the totality of the Employer’s conduct in the context of when the
bargaining occurred to determine whether the Employer engaged in bad faith. See Rutland
School Board v. Rutland Education Association, 2 VLRB 245, 273, 276 (1979). An unfair labor
practice occurs when the employee reasonably believes that the employer was making a promise
42

of benefit, such as an attractive wage offer, or a threat of reprisal. Colchester Education
Association, 19 VLRB at 111.
In Colchester, we held that the invitation to teachers to participate in a committee
studying compensation is insufficient to rise to improper circumvention of the bargaining
representative and an unfair labor practice. The coercive impact on teachers was diminished
because the committee communicating with the teachers did not include any member of the
School Board with whom the teachers were negotiating. Id. at 112.
The Board found improper communications that contained a promise of benefit where the
Employer directly communicated to staff details about a report recommending proposed job
classifications, pay rates, and backpay wage assignments. See Essex Junction Education
Association v. Essex Junction Prudential Committee, 14 VLRB 107, 125 (1991). The details of
the report had not been presented to the Union as a wage proposal, although the employer
claimed the pay rates and backpay pay rates must be negotiated with the union. Id. Employees
“could reasonably conclude that the employer was making a promise of a benefit of an attractive
wage offer. The fact that the wage offer was not actually made to the Association caused
substantial damage to the progress of good faith negotiations.” Id.
The municipal standard for determining when an employer engages in an unfair labor
practice by directly communicating with employees, was developed in conjunction with the free
speech protection provision contained in the municipal statute. See Id. at 123. (citing 21 V.S.A.
§ 1728). The language of this provision is also contained in SELRA. “The expressing of any
views, argument or opinion, or the dissemination thereof, whether in written, printed, graphic,
oral or visual form, shall not constitute or be evidence of an unfair labor practice under this
chapter, if such expression contains no threat of reprisal or force or promise of benefit.” 3
43

V.S.A. §966. The Board concludes the standard developed under the municipal statute is
consistent with SELRA and will apply it to resolve this matter.
On June 6, 2025, Commissioner Deml communicated directly with the DOC labor force.
In his “WORKFORCE MESSAGE” he outlined a “DOC Stability and Sustainability Plan”
containing five goals that included a system-wide Vermont DOC 50/50 Work/life Balance 12-
hour shift schedule, including an extended three day weekend off per pay period, a market factor
analysis to study compensation, investment in professional development, staff wellness, and data
research and analysis. After outlining the five goals in detail the Commissioner concluded,
“[t]his is the plan. It will evolve and we will adapt. But, with this roadmap in place, we can begin
this work in earnest.” Exhibit D. Commissioner Deml did not send the email to the VSEA.
In his message, the Commissioner made representations about the VSEA and its inability
or failure to work in partnership with him. “I made a series of proposals to the Vermont State
Employees Association (VSEA) to accomplish this work in partnership, but we were not able to
reach an agreement.” After claiming the Union failed to respond to his plan, the Commissioner
turned directly to employees. “So now I turn to you with our plan of action.” Exhibit D. The
Commissioner also supported his plan by referencing a survey which he claims VSEA conducted
showing that “80% of [NECC] staff supported continuation of the new 12-hour shift model.” Id.
The stipulated facts do not support nor represent that VSEA conducted such a survey. VSEA
represents that it did not conduct this survey.
Although the Commissioner recognized that implementation would require partnership
with stakeholders, including VSEA and policymakers, he did not acknowledge nor notify
employees that such topics were required subjects of bargaining or required participation and
agreement of VSEA before the plan could commence. Adding VSEA to the group of other
44

stakeholders with whom DOC seeks partnership, does not adequately chronicle the requisite
level of engagement and bargaining with the Union required before the plan could be ratified or
implemented.
On the same day Commissioner Deml distributed his email, DOC issued a press release
announcing that it “will move from 8-hour to 12-hour shifts and the state will conduct a market
factor analysis of corrections security staff pay.” Exhibit E. The press release noted that the
change was definitive and going to happen. “The schedule change will take effect . . . on August
28, 2022.” Id. The press release promises the benefit of an increase in staff pay and new
recruitment incentives for staff bringing in new employees.
Employees reading Commissioner Deml’s email and the press release could reasonably
believe that the State was promising a benefit of “50/50 Work/Life Balance 12-hour Shift
Schedule,” “increases in security staff pay,” and “new recruitment referral incentives for staff.”
The State made promises of changes to the work schedule, an increase in pay, and other benefits.
The plan was developed and communicated directly to staff. The message leads an employee to
reasonably believe that all of these benefits will happen. VSEA, in contrast, appears ineffective
or unresponsive to management’s promised benefits for employees.
The Union has demonstrated by a preponderance of the evidence that the actions of DOC
in directly communicating with the members of the unit and the public violate the duty to bargain
and interfered with the employees’ exercise of their rights in violation of 21 V.S.A. §1726 (a)(1)
and (5).
Although perhaps well intended, DOC interfered with the relationship between the
exclusive bargaining agent and the DOC employees which constitutes an unfair labor practice.
45

Rather than negotiate directly with the Union about a mandatory subject of bargaining, the
Employer communicated directly with the membership.
The State argues there was no interference because the Union did not respond to
management’s request to negotiate the impact of the decision. Management, however, never
engaged in, nor broached the topic of bargaining the mandatory subject of whether and how to
change work hours. The work hour change management represented it would implement does
not qualify as a new “workweek” as that term is defined in Article 20, Section 2. The initial
stages of the plan called for a sixty hour work week- five 12 hour shifts and two days off.
Rather than a subject of impact bargaining under Article 20, the decision or plan to move to a
twelve hour shift was a mandatory subject of bargaining.
Mr. Berard’s June 5, 2022, email did not seek negotiation on whether changes should be
made to the shifts, but rather invited the Union to negotiate the impact of the unilateral decision
management had already made. The State could not make these changes absent agreement from
the Union. The changes themselves required negotiation. Management was required to bargain
whether to change work hours, not leapfrog over this requirement to the impact of that decision.
One day after the email asking whether the Union wanted to negotiate the impacts of this change,
the Commissioner notified staff of these changes, and DOC issued a press release announcing
these changes and the date these changes would go into effect.
Management failed to engage in bargaining on the subject of whether and how to make
changes to working conditions, specifically work hours before the Commissioner communicated
his plan that the Department of Corrections “will move from 8-hour shifts to 12-hour shifts and
the State will conduct a market factor analysis of corrections security staff pay.” Exhibit D.
46

The day after Mr. Berard sent his notice to Union representatives, the Union responded
identifying the State’s misapplication of Article 20, and demanded to fully negotiate the
proposed modification to its represented employees’ work schedules, a mandatory term. Mr.
Barard immediately responded to the Union’s demand to negotiate the change in work schedule
by providing his availability to meet as soon as the following week. Exhibit I. Subsequently,
Mr. Berard retracted his July 5 communication requesting to impact bargain through Article 20
as the parties reached a side-letter pertaining to the mid-term contract modification “specifying
certain temporary schedule changes, recruitment and retention bonus and other monetary
enhancements for employees” at DOC. Exhibits H and I.
The Union claims the press release also evinces bad faith. The duty of good faith
requires “an open mind and a sincere desire to reach an agreement” and “a serious intent to
adjust difference and to reach an acceptable common ground.” See Chittenden South Education
Association, Hinesburg Unit v. Hinesburg School District and Hinesburg School Board, 8
VLRB, 219, 236 (1985), aff’d, 147 Vt. 286 (1986) (internal quotations and citations omitted).
The Board must consider the totality of the circumstances to determine whether bad faith exists.
The distribution of a plan including the date on which it would start, coupled with the false
statements about the Union and its alleged failure to respond to management offers and
initiatives, and the misstatements about a survey conducted by VSEA demonstrates bad faith.
The declarations made by DOC about its plan and the absence of any recognition or
acknowledgement that the matter was subject to mandatory bargaining with the Union does not
display the requisite serious intent to adjust the plan based on any difference with the Union or to
reach common ground. Instead, management declared “this is the plan” and when it would be
implemented.
47

Although the parties were able to reach an agreement, that does not cure nor negate the
underlying interference and failure to negotiate about a mandatory subject of bargaining. The
Employer did engage in this conduct which constitutes an unfair labor practice. The charge is
not moot because the underlying dispute that constitutes the charge is not whether to impose a
twelve hour shift, but rather whether the employer bypassed the VSEA to directly communicate
promises of benefits to the unit members and refusing to bargain with VSEA. The State does not
yet concede that it was required to negotiate with the Union representative about the subject first,
before discussing its impacts or notifying the unit members of the plan. This dispute remains
and is capable of repetition yet evading review and therefore not moot. See generally,
Burlington Firefighters Ass’n v. City of Burlington, 4 VLRB, 379, 384-85 (1981) (declining to
dismiss an unfair labor practice charge as moot where union alleged unilateral adoption of rules
and regulations of management during negotiations was refusal to bargain in good faith, despite
resolution of negotiations dispute), cited in, VSEA v. Judiciary, 35 VLRB 419, 424 (2020).
48

ORDER
Based on the foregoing findings of fact and for the foregoing reasons, it is hereby
ORDERED that the Vermont Department of Corrections Cease and Desist from communicating
directly with employees represented by the Vermont State Employees’ Association on or
regarding work hours or other mandatory subjects of bargaining.
Dated this 26th day of June 2025, at Montpelier, Vermont.
